note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Apply the describe, reflect, take action cycle

evidence.title: ERA cycle reflection on a first lab session
evidence.example: You write a short reflection on a recent learning task using the ERA cycle (Jasper 2013): experience, reflection, action. You describe what happened, reflect on why it went as it did and how you felt, and end with one action you will take next time (for example, after your first practical in a foundation year biology lab, when your results did not match the expected pattern).
evidence.artefact: A one-page reflective entry with three labelled sections, describe, reflect and take action, with tutor feedback on it.
grounding: model: ERA cycle (Jasper 2013)

evidence.title: Structured account of a customer complaint at work
evidence.example: You use the describe, reflect, take action cycle on an event from a part-time job or volunteering (for example, handling a customer complaint during a busy weekend shift in a cafe). You write what happened, think through why it unfolded that way, set one practical action, then try it on a later shift, showing you can apply the cycle to real experience.
evidence.artefact: A short structured reflective account of the work event, ending in an action, with a note on how the action went.
grounding: professional: Writes a structured reflective account of a practice event, ending in actions.
professional: NMC revalidation: written reflective accounts

genericOutcomes.title: Three-part reflection on a learning task
genericOutcomes.example: You write a short reflection on a recent learning task using a three-part cycle: describe what happened, reflect on why it went as it did and how you felt, then set one action to try next time. You keep the account tied to a single specific event rather than a general summary, so each stage builds clearly on the one before it and the action follows logically from the reflection.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A one-page entry with three labelled sections, describe, reflect and take action, kept as a record.
grounding: model: ERA cycle (Jasper 2013)

genericOutcomes.title: Structured reflection on a real incident
genericOutcomes.example: You apply the describe, reflect, take action cycle to an event from paid work or a community role. You write what happened, think through why it unfolded that way, set one practical action, then try it out the next time a similar situation arises. This shows you can carry the cycle from a written exercise into a live setting and follow it through to a change in what you do.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short structured account of a real event, ending in one action, with a note on how it went.
grounding: professional: Writes a structured reflective account of a practice event, ending in actions.
professional: NMC revalidation: written reflective accounts

genericOutcomes.title: Reflection linked to a development step
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain the describe-reflect-act cycle as a structured sequence that converts an account of an experience into a planned development step.
genericOutcomes.example: After a learning experience you set out what happened, consider why it went as it did, and identify what you will do differently. You use a simple structure, description then reflection then action, so each step depends on the last. The resulting plan links clearly back to the reflection that produced it, showing that the exercise results in a next step rather than only an account of events.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written reflection with a clear action point, structured as description, analysis and planned development.
grounding: model: ERA cycle (Jasper 2013)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Practical action plan from a real reflection
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can apply the describe-reflect-act cycle to a genuine learning experience, producing a written account that ends in one specific planned action.
genericOutcomes.example: Following a real task or incident you write a brief account of what happened, think about why, and commit to one thing to do differently next time. You then act on it in a later situation and note the result. This turns your own experience into a planned change in practice, not just a description of an event, meeting an expectation to reflect and plan ongoing development.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflective note ending in one planned action, with a follow-up note on how it went.
grounding: professional: Writes a structured reflective account of a practice event, ending in actions.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

evidence.title: Balanced evaluation table for a history presentation
evidence.example: You reflect on a piece of assessed work using the evaluation stage of Gibbs' reflective cycle (Gibbs 1988), which asks what was good and what was bad about the experience. You set out strengths first, then weaknesses, each backed by a feedback comment, so the reflection is neither wholly positive nor wholly negative (for example, a first-year history presentation where your research was praised but you ran over time).
evidence.artefact: A two-column evaluation table of strengths and weaknesses, each linked to a specific feedback comment, with a short balanced summary.
grounding: model: Gibbs' reflective cycle, evaluation stage (Gibbs 1988)

evidence.title: Fair review of a coaching session you led
evidence.example: After a real performance, you review what you did fairly and consider other ways you could have worked (for example, a sport coaching student reviewing a session run for an under-12s football club, noting that the warm-up engaged the group well but drill instructions were too long). You record both sides honestly and suggest one alternative approach for next time.
evidence.artefact: A session review sheet with balanced strengths and areas to develop, signed by the club's lead coach.
grounding: professional: Reviews own practice critically and fairly, and considers other ways of working.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect critically and consider alternative approaches

genericOutcomes.title: Balanced strengths and weaknesses review
genericOutcomes.example: You reflect on a piece of your own work using the evaluation stage of a structured reflective cycle, which asks what was good and what was less effective about the experience. You set out strengths first, then weaknesses, each backed by a specific comment or piece of feedback, so the review is neither wholly positive nor wholly negative but weighs both sides fairly before you draw a conclusion.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A two-column table of strengths and weaknesses, each linked to a specific comment, with a balanced summary.
grounding: model: Gibbs' Reflective Cycle, evaluation stage (Gibbs 1988)

genericOutcomes.title: Fair review of a session you led
genericOutcomes.example: After leading a real activity or session, you review what you did fairly, setting out what worked well alongside what did not, and consider other ways you could have approached it. You record both sides honestly rather than favouring one, back each point with a specific observation, and suggest one alternative approach you would try next time.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A review sheet listing balanced strengths and areas to develop, with a note on an alternative approach.
grounding: professional: Reviews own practice critically and fairly, and considers other ways of working.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect critically and consider alternative approaches

genericOutcomes.title: Weighing strengths and weaknesses to plan development
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain why a review of personal learning or practice should weigh strengths and weaknesses evenly before identifying a priority for development.
genericOutcomes.example: When reflecting on your own learning or practice, you deliberately set out what went well before you consider what did not, so the review covers both sides rather than only the problems. You use this balanced account to identify where effort should go next, turning an even-handed review of performance into a basis for planning further development rather than a one-sided judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A balanced written review of one piece of performance, ending in a short development point.
grounding: model: Gibbs' Reflective Cycle, evaluation stage (Gibbs 1988)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Even-handed review feeding a development plan
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can produce a balanced written review of their own performance, giving equal weight to strengths and weaknesses and ending with one development priority.
genericOutcomes.example: After a real piece of work you write a short review that gives equal attention to what went well and what did not, supporting each point with a specific example rather than a general impression. You use the balance of strengths and weaknesses to set a development priority, showing that reflecting on practice leads directly into planning what you will work on next.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written review balancing strengths and weaknesses, ending with one development priority.
grounding: professional: Reviews own practice critically and fairly, and considers other ways of working.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Notice what went well and what didn't in your own work

evidence.title: Paired in-action and on-action notes from one task
evidence.example: You keep notes during and after a task, using Schön's (1983) distinction between reflection-in-action, thinking while you are doing something, and reflection-on-action, looking back afterwards. You jot down moments where you noticed something going well or badly as it happened, then compare them with what you notice later (for example, a computing pair-programming session where you spotted a bug early but lost time on testing).
evidence.artefact: Paired notes from one task: in-the-moment jottings and a later reflection-on-action entry, with the differences highlighted.
grounding: model: Reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action (Schön 1983)

evidence.title: Session log from school reading volunteering
evidence.example: In a volunteering role, you note after each session what went well and what did not in your own contribution (for example, as a reading volunteer in a primary school, noticing that a child engaged more when you let them choose the book, but lost focus when you corrected every word). Over several sessions you spot patterns in your own work, not only in the child's.
evidence.artefact: A dated log of five or more volunteering sessions, each noting one thing that went well and one that did not.
grounding: practice: school reading volunteer scheme

genericOutcomes.title: In-action and on-action noticing
genericOutcomes.example: You keep brief notes during and after a task, drawing on the distinction between noticing things as they happen and noticing them only once you look back. While working, you jot down moments where something clearly went well or badly, then later compare those in-the-moment notes with what stands out once you have had time to think. This surfaces things you would otherwise only half remember.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Paired notes from one task, in-the-moment jottings and a later look-back entry, with differences marked.
grounding: model: Reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action (Schon 1983)

genericOutcomes.title: Session-by-session noticing log
genericOutcomes.example: Across a series of sessions doing the same kind of activity, you note straight after each one a thing that went well and a thing that did not in your own contribution, rather than focusing only on how others responded. Over several sessions you look back across the notes and spot patterns in your own approach, not just in isolated single events, building a clearer picture of your own habits.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A dated log of five or more sessions, each noting one strength and one weakness in your own contribution.
grounding: professional: Notices patterns in own contribution across repeated sessions of practice.

genericOutcomes.title: Spotting what worked in your own work
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain why reviewing their own work means identifying specific strengths and weaknesses separately rather than forming one overall impression.
genericOutcomes.example: Looking back at a piece of your own work, you separate out what went well from what did not, rather than treating the outcome as simply good or bad overall. You identify at least one specific strength and one specific weakness, each tied to a particular part of what you did, so the noticing is concrete rather than a vague overall feeling about how things went.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note identifying one specific strength and one specific weakness in a piece of your own work.
grounding: model: Reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action (Schon 1983)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Noticing strengths and gaps after a task
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify, in a piece of their own completed work, one specific strength and one specific weakness before receiving feedback from others.
genericOutcomes.example: Straight after completing a real task, you take a moment to identify one thing in your own work that went well and one thing that did not, before anyone else gives you feedback. You record both briefly so you are forming your own view of your performance first, rather than only reacting to what others tell you about it later.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A brief self-written note naming one strength and one gap, made before receiving outside feedback.
grounding: professional: Notices patterns in own contribution across repeated sessions of practice.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

evidence.title: Reflective entry rewritten from descriptive to critical
evidence.example: You take an earlier reflective entry and rewrite it using Hatton and Smith's (1995) four types of reflective writing: descriptive writing, descriptive reflection, dialogic reflection and critical reflection. You label the type each paragraph shows, then revise the descriptive passages so they question your reasons, weigh other explanations and consider the wider context (for example, a social work student's entry on a shadowed home visit that recounted events but never asked why the family seemed wary).
evidence.artefact: Original and revised reflective entries, with each paragraph labelled by type and a note on what changed between them.
grounding: model: Four types of reflective writing (Hatton and Smith 1995)

evidence.title: Critical placement reflection discussed with a practice educator
evidence.example: You reflect critically on your practice in a real setting, asking why you acted as you did and what else you could have done (for example, a diagnostic radiography student on placement who rushed a patient's positioning, and reflects on time pressure, communication and the alternatives). You move beyond recounting the event to judging it against the standards expected of you.
evidence.artefact: A placement reflective account discussed with your practice educator, with their written comments on the depth of reflection.
grounding: professional: Reflects critically on own practice and considers alternative approaches.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect critically and consider alternative approaches

genericOutcomes.title: Reflective writing revised from descriptive to critical
genericOutcomes.example: You take an earlier reflective entry and rewrite it using a framework of four types of reflective writing: description, descriptive reflection, dialogic reflection and critical reflection. You label which type each paragraph currently shows, then revise the descriptive passages so they question your reasons, weigh other possible explanations and consider the wider context, rather than simply recounting what happened.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Original and revised reflective entries, each paragraph labelled by type, with notes on what changed.
grounding: model: Four types of reflective writing (Hatton and Smith 1995)

genericOutcomes.title: Critical reflection discussed with a reviewer
genericOutcomes.example: You reflect critically on a real piece of your own practice, asking why you acted as you did and what else you could have done, rather than only describing the sequence of events. Someone experienced in the area reviews your account and comments on its depth. You revise the entry to move beyond recounting what happened, judging it instead against the standard expected.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A reflective account reviewed by an experienced colleague, with their written comments on the depth shown.
grounding: professional: Reflects critically on own practice and considers alternative approaches.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect critically and consider alternative approaches

genericOutcomes.title: Moving from description to critical judgement
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse a descriptive account of their own practice to identify the assumptions and reasoning underlying what happened, producing a critical judgement rather than a narrative.
genericOutcomes.example: Given an account of your own learning or practice, you rewrite the descriptive parts so that each one is followed by a question about why things happened that way, what assumptions were at work, and what else might explain the outcome. The revised version makes a judgement supported by reasoning, rather than only reporting a sequence of events, directly extending reflection into planning what to do differently.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short piece of writing where each descriptive statement is paired with a critical question and judgement.
grounding: model: Four types of reflective writing (Hatton and Smith 1995)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Critical account of a real decision
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate a real decision by examining the alternatives considered and the reasoning behind it, justifying what they would do differently.
genericOutcomes.example: After a real decision or action, you write an account that goes beyond what happened to ask why you chose that course, what alternatives existed, and how your reasoning stands up to scrutiny. You identify at least one thing you would do differently and justify the change. This shows reflection feeding directly into a judgement about your own development rather than stopping at a narrative.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written account of a decision that states the alternatives considered and the judgement reached.
grounding: professional: Reflects critically on own practice and considers alternative approaches.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Turn reflection into a dated action plan

evidence.title: SMART action plan drawn from a reflection
evidence.example: You turn a reflection into an action plan using SMART objectives (Doran 1981): specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related. You rewrite vague intentions such as managing time better into dated actions, and justify why each one follows from what the reflection found (for example, an engineering student planning to book two lab slots by set dates before a design report deadline).
evidence.artefact: An action plan table of dated SMART actions, each linked to a line in the reflection, with a review column.
grounding: model: SMART objectives (Doran 1981)

evidence.title: Dated development targets after a mentor observation
evidence.example: You turn reflection from a placement into a dated development plan that someone else reviews (for example, a trainee teacher on school placement who, after a mentor observation, sets dated targets on questioning and classroom routines for the next four weeks). You choose which targets matter most and explain why, then record progress at each review date.
evidence.artefact: The dated development plan with progress notes, initialled by your school mentor at each review.
grounding: professional: Plans and records development actions from reflection on practice.
professional: Social Work England professional standards 4.6

genericOutcomes.title: SMART action plan from a reflection
genericOutcomes.example: You turn a reflection on your own performance into an action plan using a framework of specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related objectives. You rewrite vague intentions, such as managing time better, into dated actions, and for each one you justify why it follows from something the reflection identified, so the plan is clearly tied to what you learned about yourself.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An action plan table of dated objectives, each linked to a line in the reflection, with a review column.
grounding: model: SMART objectives (Doran 1981)

genericOutcomes.title: Dated targets after an observed session
genericOutcomes.example: Following a real session that someone else observed, you turn the resulting feedback and your own reflection into a short set of dated targets covering the next few weeks. You decide which targets matter most and explain your reasoning, then record progress against each one at agreed review points, so the plan is checked rather than simply written and forgotten.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A dated development plan with progress notes, reviewed and initialled at each agreed check-in point.
grounding: professional: Plans and records development actions from reflection on practice.
professional: Social Work England professional standards 4.6

genericOutcomes.title: Turning a reflection into a dated plan
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how a reflection on learning or practice should be converted into one or more dated, checkable actions that follow logically from what was noticed.
genericOutcomes.example: Once you have reflected on a piece of learning or practice, you convert the main point into one or more actions, each with its own date and a way of checking it has been done. You explain how each action follows from the reflection, so a reader can trace a line from what you noticed to what you plan to change, rather than the two sitting separately.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflection paired with a dated action, each action traceable back to a specific point raised.
grounding: model: SMART objectives (Doran 1981)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Dated plan built from a real reflection
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a dated action plan from a real reflection, then record on the stated date whether the action was completed and what changed.
genericOutcomes.example: After reflecting on a real piece of work, you set one or more dated actions that follow directly from what the reflection found, rather than generic good intentions. You record a date by which each action will be completed, then return to the plan on that date to note whether it was done and what difference it made, closing the loop between reflecting and acting.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A dated action plan drawn from a real reflection, with a follow-up note on completion and effect.
grounding: professional: Plans and records development actions from reflection on practice.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Reflect on motivation and amend strategies that aren't working

evidence.title: Self-regulation review of a failing revision strategy
evidence.example: You analyse a study strategy that is not working using Zimmerman's (2002) cyclical model of self-regulated learning, with its forethought, performance and self-reflection phases. You track your motivation and results over a few weeks, find where the cycle breaks down, and change the strategy, justifying the change with your own evidence (for example, a mathematics student who swaps rereading lecture notes for timed problem sheets after weak tutorial scores).
evidence.artefact: A strategy review with several weeks of tracking data, your analysis by phase, and the amended plan with its results.
grounding: model: Cyclical model of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002)

evidence.title: Changing a work routine after supervision feedback
evidence.example: You use feedback or supervision in a real role to find out what is not working and change how you work (for example, a psychology student employed as a research assistant who learns in supervision that data entry errors come from rushing late in the day, and moves checking to the morning). You reflect on what was driving your motivation and record whether the change worked.
evidence.artefact: Supervision notes or feedback, your follow-up reflection, and a record showing the effect of the changed approach.
grounding: professional: Uses feedback and supervision to find learning needs and change how one works.
professional: Vitae RDF B1 Personal qualities: self-reflection

genericOutcomes.title: Self-regulation review of a failing strategy
genericOutcomes.example: You analyse a strategy that is not producing the results you want, using a cyclical model of self-regulated learning with forethought, performance and self-reflection phases. You track your own motivation and your results over several attempts, identify where the cycle is breaking down, and change the strategy, justifying the change with evidence you have gathered yourself rather than a hunch.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A strategy review with tracking data over several attempts, analysis by phase, and the amended plan.
grounding: model: Cyclical model of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002)

genericOutcomes.title: Changing a routine after feedback
genericOutcomes.example: Using feedback or supervision in a real role, you find out what in your current approach is not working and change how you do it. You reflect on what was affecting your motivation at the time, make one concrete change to your routine, and record over the following weeks whether the change actually improved things, rather than assuming it has.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Feedback notes, a short follow-up reflection, and a record showing the effect of the changed approach.
grounding: professional: Uses feedback and supervision to find learning needs and change how one works.
professional: Vitae RDF B1 Personal qualities: self-reflection

genericOutcomes.title: Adjusting a learning strategy using reflection
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse why a learning strategy is not working, distinguishing a drop in motivation from a flaw in the approach itself, to justify a specific change.
genericOutcomes.example: When a way of working is not delivering the results you expect, you reflect on both your motivation and the strategy itself, rather than assuming the problem is only effort. You identify the point where the approach breaks down, design a specific change, and set out how you will know, from your own evidence, whether the new approach is actually working better than the old one.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written comparison of the old and new strategy, with evidence for which one worked better.
grounding: model: Cyclical model of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Reflecting on motivation to change an approach
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate a real approach that is not delivering results, make one specific change, and judge from the outcome whether to keep it.
genericOutcomes.example: In a real piece of work, you notice that your motivation has dropped or that a way of working is not producing good results, and you reflect on why before deciding what to change. You make one specific adjustment, keep working at it for a set period, then judge from the outcome whether to keep the change, drop it, or adjust it again.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflective note on motivation and strategy, with the change made and its later outcome.
grounding: professional: Uses feedback and supervision to find learning needs and change how one works.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Choose and apply a fuller model (Gibbs, Kolb, Johns)

evidence.title: Assessed reflection with a justified choice of model
evidence.example: You write an assessed reflection after comparing three models: Gibbs' (1988) six-stage reflective cycle, Kolb's (1984) four-stage experiential learning cycle, and Johns' (1995) model of structured reflection, which draws on Carper's ways of knowing. You choose one, justify why it suits this experience, and apply it fully (for example, a midwifery student choosing Johns for an emotionally demanding birth, because its cue questions explore personal and ethical knowing).
evidence.artefact: An assessed reflective essay with a short rationale section comparing the three models and explaining your choice.
grounding: ing:doc:reflective-cycle-gibbs-1988
ing:doc:experiential-learning-kolb-1984
ing:doc:structured-reflection-johns-1995

evidence.title: Employer reflection template mapped to a named model
evidence.example: You use the reflective model or form your profession or employer expects for a real event, and justify how you applied it (for example, a paramedic science student completing the ambulance service's reflection template after a difficult call, and mapping its prompts to Gibbs' stages). Where the form is fixed, you show how you still reflected in depth within it.
evidence.artefact: A completed reflective template from placement, with a short note mapping its prompts to a named model, reviewed by your mentor.
grounding: professional: Uses the reflective model the profession or employer expects, and justifies the choice.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect on and review practice

genericOutcomes.title: Justified choice between three reflective models
genericOutcomes.example: You compare three different reflective models, each with its own stages and emphasis, for example one with six structured stages, one with four stages built around experience and experimentation, and one that explores different kinds of knowing. You choose the model that best fits a particular experience, justify the choice, and apply it fully rather than following its stages only loosely.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A reflective piece with a short rationale comparing the three models and explaining your eventual choice.
grounding: ing:doc:reflective-cycle-gibbs-1988
ing:doc:experiential-learning-kolb-1984
ing:doc:structured-reflection-johns-1995

genericOutcomes.title: Reflective template mapped to a named model
genericOutcomes.example: You use whatever reflective template or form a real setting requires, even when its headings do not match any single published model exactly. After completing it for a real event, you map its prompts onto the stages of a named reflective model and note where the fixed form still allowed you to reflect in depth, showing you can work within an imposed structure rather than only a freely chosen one.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A completed reflective template with a short note mapping its prompts to a named model, with a reviewer comment.
grounding: professional: Uses the reflective model the profession or employer expects, and justifies the choice.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect on and review practice

genericOutcomes.title: Applying a chosen reflective model to a real problem
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify the choice of one established reflective model over its alternatives for a given situation, then construct a reflection that works through every stage of that model.
genericOutcomes.example: Faced with a specific experience that needs more than a quick note, you select one established reflective model from several available, explain briefly why its structure suits this particular situation better than the alternatives, and then work through every one of its stages in full. This shows applying a chosen framework of knowledge to a real situation, rather than describing the models in the abstract.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A worked reflection following every stage of one named model, with a short note on why it was chosen.
grounding: ing:doc:reflective-cycle-gibbs-1988
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/applying-knowledge-to-practice-or-problems

genericOutcomes.title: Applying a required reflective structure in practice
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can apply a required reflective structure fully to a genuine event, critique how closely their response matches a recognised model's stages, and note where the structure constrained their reflection.
genericOutcomes.example: In a real setting you are often given a fixed reflective structure to use rather than a free choice of model. You apply it fully to a genuine event, then check that your answers actually match a recognised model's stages rather than drifting into description, and note any point where the required structure limited how deep your reflection could go.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A completed reflection in a required format, checked against a named model's stages, with notes on limits.
grounding: professional: Uses the reflective model the profession or employer expects, and justifies the choice.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/applying-knowledge-to-practice-or-problems

capabilities.statement: Use reflection for CPD and lifelong learning

evidence.title: Term-long CPD log of linked Kolb cycles
evidence.example: You build a reflective CPD record over a term, using Kolb's (1984) experiential learning cycle to link entries: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation, with each experiment becoming the next experience. You show how repeated cycles add up to development over time rather than one-off reflections (for example, an accountancy student preparing for professional body CPD by tracking growth in client communication).
evidence.artefact: A term-long CPD log of linked cycles, with a summary showing how your practice changed across the entries.
grounding: ing:doc:experiential-learning-kolb-1984

evidence.title: CPD portfolio section mapped to professional standards
evidence.example: You record reflection as CPD evidence in the format a regulator or employer uses (for example, a nursing student writing practice reflective accounts in the style of NMC revalidation, or a graduate teaching assistant mapping reflections to the Advance HE Professional Standards Framework). You select entries that show development, link each to the relevant standard, and discuss them with a peer.
evidence.artefact: A CPD portfolio section with reflective accounts mapped to named standards, and a record of the peer discussion.
grounding: professional: Records reflection on learning and practice as CPD evidence, to a regulator's or employer's standard.
professional: NMC revalidation
professional: Advance HE PSF 2023 A5

genericOutcomes.title: Linked reflective cycles building a CPD record
genericOutcomes.example: You build a reflective record over an extended period, using a four-stage experiential learning cycle, concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract thinking and active experimentation, to link entries together so each experiment becomes the starting point for the next cycle. The record shows cumulative development across repeated cycles, rather than a series of separate, unconnected reflections on single events.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A term-long log of linked reflective cycles, with a summary of how your practice changed across entries.
grounding: ing:doc:experiential-learning-kolb-1984

genericOutcomes.title: CPD portfolio mapped to professional standards
genericOutcomes.example: You record ongoing reflection as evidence of continuing professional development, in whatever format a relevant professional body or employer expects. You select entries that show real development over time, link each one explicitly to a named standard it demonstrates, and discuss a selection of them with a peer to check the development is genuine rather than only self-reported.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A CPD portfolio section with reflective entries mapped to named standards and a note of a peer discussion.
grounding: professional: Records reflection on learning and practice as CPD evidence, to a regulator's or employer's standard.
professional: NMC revalidation

genericOutcomes.title: Reflection sustained across a career-long record
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can synthesise several linked cycles of reflection into a single account that demonstrates a trajectory of development sustained beyond the point of qualifying.
genericOutcomes.example: You treat reflection as an ongoing record rather than a single exercise, using a cycle in which each completed experiment becomes the starting experience for the next round of reflection. Looking back across several linked cycles, you can show a trajectory of development in a specific area of practice, demonstrating preparation for a professional setting where development continues well beyond the point of qualifying.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A reflective record spanning several linked cycles, with a short summary of the development trajectory shown.
grounding: ing:doc:experiential-learning-kolb-1984
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/professional-practice-and-employability

genericOutcomes.title: CPD evidence prepared for professional settings
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a running record of reflection on their own practice, in a professional format, linking each entry to a specific external standard.
genericOutcomes.example: You keep a running record of reflection on your practice in the format expected in a professional setting, rather than only for a single piece of coursework. Each entry links what happened to a specific standard or expectation of that setting, and over time the collection demonstrates readiness for ongoing professional development, not just a one-off reflective skill shown for an assessment.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A running CPD record in a professional format, each entry linked to a specific external standard.
grounding: professional: Records reflection on learning and practice as CPD evidence, to a regulator's or employer's standard.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/professional-practice-and-employability

capabilities.statement: Reflexivity: how your identity and values shape what you notice

evidence.title: Reflexive commentary using Finlay's variants of reflexivity
evidence.example: You examine how your identity, values and position shape what you notice, using Finlay's (2002) variants of reflexivity: introspection, intersubjective reflection, mutual collaboration, social critique and discursive deconstruction. You choose the variants that fit and show how your background led you to see some things and miss others (for example, a master's student in development studies reflecting on how being an outsider shaped interviews with farmers during fieldwork).
evidence.artefact: A reflexive commentary or methodological appendix naming the variants used, with field note extracts showing their effect.
grounding: ing:doc:variants-of-reflexivity-finlay-2002

evidence.title: Supervision reflection on values shaping a risk judgement
evidence.example: You challenge how your own values affect your practice and the people you work with (for example, a postgraduate social work student realising in supervision that their views about family stability influenced a risk assessment, and asking a colleague to review it). You record what you noticed, what you changed, and how you will keep checking your assumptions in future cases.
evidence.artefact: An anonymised supervision reflection showing the value identified, its effect on your judgement, and the action you took.
grounding: professional: Reflects on own values and challenges their effect on practice.
professional: Social Work England professional standards 4.8

genericOutcomes.title: Naming which variant of reflexivity applies
genericOutcomes.example: You examine how your own identity, values and position shape what you notice, choosing from several named variants of reflexivity, for example turning attention onto your own reactions, reflecting on the relationship with others involved, working collaboratively to check an interpretation, or stepping back to question the assumptions built into how you are looking at something. You show how your background led you to notice some things and miss others.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A reflexive commentary naming the variants used, with specific extracts showing their effect on what you noticed.
grounding: ing:doc:variants-of-reflexivity-finlay-2002

genericOutcomes.title: Challenging a value shaping a real judgement
genericOutcomes.example: In discussion with someone experienced in the area, you realise that one of your own values or assumptions has influenced a real judgement you made about a situation or a person. You record what you noticed, how you changed the judgement or asked someone else to check it, and what you will do to keep testing your own assumptions in similar situations in future.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An anonymised reflection naming the value identified, its effect on the judgement, and the action taken.
grounding: professional: Reflects on own values and challenges their effect on practice.
professional: Social Work England professional standards 4.8

genericOutcomes.title: Examining personal responsibility in reflective judgement
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique a judgement they reached about a real situation by examining how their own identity, assumptions or social position may have shaped it, using a named approach to reflexivity.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a judgement or interpretation you reached about a real situation and ask how your own identity, assumptions or social position might have shaped it, rather than treating the judgement as neutral. Using a named approach to reflexivity, you pick out which aspect of your own standpoint was most likely to be at work, and set out what a different standpoint might have noticed instead.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written analysis naming your standpoint, its likely effect, and what an alternative standpoint might show.
grounding: ing:doc:variants-of-reflexivity-finlay-2002
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/1.11

genericOutcomes.title: Testing how personal values affect a decision
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify a real decision by checking whether a personal value, rather than the available evidence, is driving the judgement, and set out how they will keep checking for this.
genericOutcomes.example: Before acting on a real judgement, you pause to ask whether a personal value or assumption of yours, rather than the evidence in front of you, is driving the decision. You check this with someone else where possible, note what you found, and record how you will keep checking for this kind of influence in similar decisions, treating personal responsibility as part of making the judgement, not separate from it.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note recording a checked judgement, the value identified, and the plan to keep checking it.
grounding: professional: Reflects on own values and challenges their effect on practice.
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/1.11
